title: The Invention of Velcro
summary: The story of how a curious walk in the woods and some sticky seed pods led George de Mestral to invent Velcro, a hook-and-loop fastener copied from nature.
poll: Nature itself was the real inventor of Velcro, since George de Mestral only copied what a simple plant already does.

versions.title: The Invention of Velcro
versions.text:
Long ago, there was no Velcro. A man went for a walk. His name was George de Mestral. He walked his dog in the woods.

Small seed pods from a plant stuck to his socks. They stuck to his dog's fur too. He looked at one closely. It had tiny hooks.

George had an idea. What if he made a strip with hooks? What if he made another strip with loops? The hooks would catch the loops. The two strips would stick together.

It took George many years to make it work. He kept trying. At last, he made two matching strips. One had small hooks. One had soft loops.

He named it Velcro. The name came from two French words. One word meant velvet. One word meant hook.

Today, Velcro is used all over the world. It is on shoes, bags, and coats. It is even used on space suits!

versions.title: The Invention of Velcro

Long ago, there was no such thing as Velcro. A man named George de Mestral liked to take long walks with his dog through the woods near his home. One day, he came home covered in small, sticky seed pods.

The seed pods, from a prickly plant, clung tightly to his socks and clothing. They also clung stubbornly to his dog's thick fur. Curious about why they stuck so well, he examined one closely under a magnifying glass. It had tiny hooks curling outward from every side.

George had a genuinely clever idea. What if he made one strip covered in tiny hooks, and another strip covered in soft loops? The hooks could catch onto the loops easily. The two strips would stick together. This was just like the seed pods had stuck to his socks.

Turning this simple idea into a real product took George many years of hard effort. He tested many materials and designs. At last, he found one that worked. He created two matching strips that gripped together reliably.

He named his invention Velcro, combining two French words. One word meant velvet, and the other meant hook. This fit the soft, looped side and the hooked side perfectly.

Today, Velcro is used by people all over the world. It appears on shoes, bags, and coats nearly everywhere. It is even used on space suits during real missions into outer space.

versions.title: The Invention of Velcro
versions.text:
For as long as people can remember, fastening things required buttons, laces, or buckles. In the 1940s, a man named George de Mestral took his dog for a long walk through the woods near his home in Switzerland.

When he returned, both he and his dog were covered in small, sticky seed pods called burrs. The burrs clung tightly to his socks and to his dog's fur. They were surprisingly hard to pull off. He was curious why they stuck so well. De Mestral examined one closely under a magnifying glass. He discovered that each burr was covered in tiny, curved hooks.

De Mestral wanted to copy what he saw. What if he created one fabric strip covered in tiny hooks? What if he made a second strip covered in small, soft loops? The hooks would catch onto the loops. This was just like the burr's hooks had caught onto the loops in his sock's fabric.

Turning this simple idea into a working product took de Mestral many years of effort. He experimented with many materials. At last, he found ones sturdy enough to use. He perfected two matching strips that gripped together firmly. They could be pulled apart and reused.

He named his invention Velcro, a word built from two French words meaning velvet and hook. The clothing industry was slow to notice the invention at first. That would soon change.

Today, Velcro and similar hook-and-loop fasteners are used worldwide, appearing on shoes, bags, coats, and even on astronauts' space suits during missions in outer space.

Curious why they adhered so stubbornly to almost everything, de Mestral examined a single burr under a microscope. He discovered that it was covered in dozens of curved, hooked spines, shaped by nature to cling to passing animals and disperse seeds.

He tested countless materials before settling on a synthetic fabric durable enough for everyday, repeated use. Eventually he perfected two matching strips that gripped together firmly yet could be pulled apart and reused, and he secured a patent for the finished design, unlike ordinary glue or other sticky adhesive.

He named his invention Velcro, combining two French words meaning velvet and hook. The clothing industry was slow to notice this unusual new fastener at first, but that reluctance would soon change as manufacturers discovered its remarkable usefulness.

Today, Velcro and similar hook-and-loop fasteners are used worldwide, appearing on shoes, bags, coats, and even on astronauts' space suits during missions far beyond Earth's atmosphere.
